title: Donald and Ivana Trump marry; alleged prenup terms remain unverified
description_medium: Donald Trump and Ivana Zelníčková married in 1977. Their marriage later became the subject of a public divorce dispute, and Donald Trump discussed their prenuptial agreement in interviews in 1990 and 1994. The supplied timeline claims the agreement required three children and promised Ivana $1 million if they divorced, but the linked reporting does not establish those specific terms.
description_long: Donald Trump and Ivana Zelníčková married in 1977, beginning a marriage that became a matter of public attention as Donald Trump’s New York real-estate profile grew. The couple had three children. When the marriage ended, their financial settlement and the prenuptial agreement became subjects of press coverage and litigation. In later television interviews, Trump acknowledged the agreement and said Ivana had challenged it for several years, but those comments do not substantiate every reported clause. The linked timeline asserts that the contract required the couple to have three children and guaranteed Ivana $1 million in a divorce. The accessible linked newspaper story discusses fine print in the divorce dispute but does not verify those exact provisions. Trump's later remarks confirm that a prenuptial agreement existed and was contested, but they do not settle these details. The alleged clauses therefore remain unverified.
evidence_notes: The marriage and three children are documented biographical facts; the existence and litigation of a prenup are supported by Trump’s interviews. Neither linked story establishes the specific three-child clause or $1 million guarantee. The revised title removes those unverified contractual assertions.
corrected_wording: Retitled to avoid presenting the alleged prenup terms as established. Retain the claim only if the agreement or reliable reporting verifies its language.
exact_blocker: The supplied TrumpFile entry and linked 1990 New York Times article do not establish that the prenup required three children or guaranteed Ivana $1 million upon divorce.

title: Donald Trump Jr. is born
description_medium: Donald Trump Jr. was born in New York City on December 31, 1977, the first child of Donald and Ivana Trump. His maternal grandparents lived near Prague, and he spent childhood summers with them, learning Czech and developing a close relationship with his grandfather Miloš Zelníček. These early family details provide context for his upbringing without attributing later political activity to his birth.
description_long: Donald John Trump Jr. was born in New York City on December 31, 1977, to Donald and Ivana Trump. He was the couple’s first child; Ivanka and Eric were born later. Biographical accounts describe a childhood divided between New York and visits to his maternal family in Czechoslovakia. Trump Jr. spent summers near Prague with his grandfather Miloš Zelníček, learned Czech, and recalled those visits as especially memorable. Those details help situate the birth within the family story and explain the Czech-language and Central European background that appears in accounts of his early years. The available biographies emphasize his grandparents’ influence and the recurring summer visits as features of his childhood. The birth itself does not establish anything about his later political role. This entry is limited to the birth and the immediate family context reported in the linked biography and timeline.
evidence_notes: The birth date and parents are directly stated by Biography.com and the supplied timeline. GQ provides the grandfather recollection; retain the event title and leave unrelated metadata untouched.
corrected_wording: Added a medium and long description grounding the birth in biographical details about his parents and maternal grandfather; did not extend the record into later political activity.

title: Roy Cohn introduces Roger Stone to Donald Trump and Fred Trump
description_medium: Roger Stone recalled first meeting Donald Trump in 1979 through lawyer Roy Cohn, with Trump’s father Fred also present. Stone was then a 26-year-old aide working on Ronald Reagan’s presidential campaign. The introduction began a long association between Stone and Trump, though it does not establish when Trump first met Stone’s later business partner Paul Manafort.
description_long: Roger Stone has said that his first meeting with Donald Trump took place in 1979, when Stone was a 26-year-old aide working for Ronald Reagan’s presidential campaign. Lawyer Roy Cohn arranged the introduction, and Trump’s father Fred was also there. Stone described recognizing Cohn among the people at the gathering and credited the connection with bringing him into Trump’s orbit. The episode is an early point in the relationship between Stone, a Republican political operative, and Trump, a New York real-estate developer. Stone later remained involved in Trump’s political world, including during his presidential ambitions. The timeline’s further suggestion that Trump met Paul Manafort soon afterward is an inference: Stone and Manafort’s business partnership began in 1980, but that does not date a first meeting between Trump and Manafort. The account supports the Cohn introduction and the presence of Fred Trump, not the inferred Manafort chronology.
evidence_notes: New Yorker’s interview/profile supports the 1979 first meeting, Cohn introduction, and Reagan campaign context. The entry correctly treats the date as year-specific rather than a precise day. The later Manafort meeting is not established by the 1980 partnership.
corrected_wording: Removed the speculative assertion that Trump met Manafort shortly after Stone; title clarified the documented introduction.

title: A later compilation lists more than 1,000 past and present Council for National Policy members
description_medium: The Council for National Policy was formed in 1981 as a private umbrella group for conservative political figures and organizers. A later TrumpFile compilation lists 1,011 people associated with the organization between 1981 and 2020, while warning that it may include fewer than half of its members. The list alone does not establish Donald Trump’s membership or a specific connection to his administration.
description_long: The Council for National Policy began in 1981, when conservative activists and political figures established an umbrella organization for discussion and coordination. A New York Times report at the time described the group’s creation and its organizers’ hope that it would become influential. Decades later, the TrumpFile timeline published a compilation of 1,011 names connected with the council across the period from 1981 to 2020. The page itself cautions that its roster may represent fewer than half of the organization’s members. A name compilation spanning nearly four decades is not a membership register with dates, roles, or attendance records. It therefore cannot show when a person joined, what that person did within the group, or whether any particular policy resulted from the council’s activity. The supplied synopsis names several political figures but does not document Donald Trump as a member or participant. The entry can describe the organization and the existence of the list; the specific Trump connection remains unverified.
evidence_notes: Contemporaneous NYT reporting supports the group’s formation; the TrumpFile page is the source for the later 1,011-name compilation and its incompleteness caveat. No source in the supplied material establishes Trump’s membership, so title and descriptions avoid implying it.
corrected_wording: Retitled to center the verifiable subject, the later membership compilation, rather than imply that it proves Trump’s participation.
exact_blocker: No supplied source establishes Donald Trump’s membership or role in the Council for National Policy; the entry remains a list-description record rather than a documented Trump event.

title: Jeffrey Epstein starts a financial consulting business after leaving Bear Stearns
description_medium: A TrumpFile timeline dates Jeffrey Epstein’s launch of Intercontinental Assets Group Inc. to August 18, 1981, after his work at Bear Stearns. It describes the firm as a consultancy that claimed to recover funds for clients from brokers and lawyers accused of fraud. EBSCO’s biography dates the start of his consulting company to 1982 and calls it International Assets Group. The available sources do not establish the allegations about intelligence agencies or organized crime in the former title.
description_long: Jeffrey Epstein worked at Bear Stearns before moving into private financial consulting. The TrumpFile timeline dates the launch of Intercontinental Assets Group Inc. to August 18, 1981, and describes its work as helping clients recover money from brokers and lawyers accused of fraud. EBSCO’s biographical account gives a different year, 1982, and refers to the business as International Assets Group. The available material therefore supports the broad transition from Wall Street employment to a consulting venture but leaves the exact date and company name inconsistent. The timeline’s former title linked the business to Ghislaine Maxwell, Semion Mogilevich, Mossad, and the CIA. No evidence supplied here substantiates those claims, and they should not be inferred from the company’s name or Epstein’s later notoriety. Nor does this material document a connection between the consulting firm and Donald Trump. This description stays with the limited business-history evidence and preserves the discrepancy for resolution.
evidence_notes: TrumpFile dates the launch to 1981 and uses Intercontinental Assets Group; EBSCO dates a consulting company to 1982 and calls it International Assets Group. The date/name need source resolution. The former title's intelligence and organized-crime claims are unsupported by the supplied sources.
corrected_wording: Retitled to remove sensational claims about Maxwell, Mogilevich, Mossad and the CIA, which the available sources do not establish.
exact_blocker: Sources disagree on the consulting venture’s year (1981 versus 1982) and name (Intercontinental versus International Assets Group); neither supplied source supports the former title’s intelligence or organized-crime claims.
